title: Advanced experimentation | Prompt & context engineering
objectives: Use variance reduction and sequential methods correctly. Engineer prompts and context systematically rather than by trial and error.
exercise: Simulate an A/B test with a revenue metric and compare naive vs CUPED confidence-interval widths. Then build a prompt that extracts structured fields (merchant, amount, category) from 50 messy transaction descriptions, and measure exact-match accuracy.
resources: Spotify Engineering, Choosing a Sequential Testing Framework (2023)
Johari et al., Always Valid Inference (arXiv:1512.04922)
AI Engineering, Ch. 5 (prompt engineering, defensive prompting)

cards.q: If corr(pre, post) = 0.7, by what percentage does CUPED reduce variance?
cards.explain: Variance falls by ρ² = 0.49, so 49%; the adjusted variance is (1 − ρ²) = 51% of the original. (The curriculum's '≈51%' is the remaining share, not the reduction.)

cards.q: corr(pre, post) = 0.7. What percentage of the original variance remains after CUPED?
In CUPED, Y_adj = Y − θ(X − X̄). What is θ?
cards.explain: It's the OLS slope of Y on X.

cards.q: Cov(Y, X) = 12, Var(X) = 20. What is θ?
What does CUPED do to the treatment effect estimate?
choices: Keeps it unbiased and reduces its variance
cards.explain: E[X] is the same in both arms (pre-period), so the adjustment subtracts mean-zero noise.

cards.q: With corr(pre, post) = 0.7, the CUPED-adjusted test needs what fraction of the original sample size for the same power? (decimal)
Why is using in-experiment activity as the CUPED covariate invalid?
cards.answer: The covariate must be unaffected by treatment. In-experiment activity can be changed by the treatment, so X̄ differs between arms. The adjustment then subtracts part of the real treatment effect (or adds bias). Pre-experiment data is independent of assignment by construction.
rubric: Covariate must be independent of treatment
In-experiment X is affected by treatment → bias
Pre-period data is safe by randomisation

cards.q: Usually the best CUPED covariate is…
choices: The same metric measured in the pre-experiment period
The metric measured during week 1 of the test

cards.q: A test targets brand-new sign-ups. How much will CUPED (pre-period metric) help?
choices: Little: new users have no pre-period history, so ρ ≈ 0
A lot: new users are homogeneous
cards.explain: Consider other pre-assignment covariates (acquisition channel, device).

cards.q: CUPED is essentially equivalent to…
choices: Regression adjustment (ANCOVA) with the pre-period covariate

cards.q: Some users lack pre-period data. A valid approach?
choices: Fill a constant (e.g. 0 or the mean) plus a missing-indicator covariate; assignment is still independent
Drop those users from treatment only
Abandon CUPED for the whole test

cards.q: Group sequential vs always-valid: which keeps more power with a fixed schedule of 5 analyses?
cards.explain: Always-valid tests pay for unlimited looks; GSTs spend α only at the planned looks (Spotify's reasoning).

cards.q: Why does peeking at a fixed-horizon test inflate false positives?
choices: Each look is another chance to cross the threshold by noise; stopping at the first crossing compounds them

cards.q: Checking a fixed-horizon test daily for a month and stopping at the first p < 0.05 gives a false-positive rate of roughly…
An O'Brien–Fleming-type alpha spending function…
choices: Spends very little α at early looks and most at the final analysis
Spends α equally at each look
Spends all α at the first look

cards.q: Main benefit of always-valid inference (mSPRT)?
choices: Valid p-values/CIs at any stopping time, even with continuous monitoring
Highest power at a fixed horizon
Removes the need for SRM checks

cards.q: Why might a rider-side pricing test at Grab bias results through driver supply, and what design mitigates it?
cards.answer: Treatment and control riders share the same driver pool. If the treatment's lower prices increase demand, treated riders absorb drivers, which raises control riders' wait times and cancellations. Control is contaminated (a SUTVA violation), and the estimated effect is overstated. Mitigate with switchback (time-sliced within a region) or geo/cluster randomisation so each market is fully treated or fully control.

cards.q: SUTVA requires that…
choices: Each unit's outcome depends only on its own treatment (no interference) and there is one version of treatment
Treatment and control have equal size

cards.q: Main threat in a switchback design, and the usual fix?
choices: Carryover between periods; add washout/buffer windows and choose period length carefully

cards.q: Why keep a long-term holdout group?
choices: To measure the cumulative long-run impact of shipped features (and catch effects that decay or grow)
To increase power for the next test

cards.q: You slice the result by 12 segments and one shows a big effect. Main caution?
choices: Multiple comparisons: treat it as a hypothesis for a follow-up test, not a finding

cards.q: Name four components of a production system prompt.
cards.answer: Role/persona; task and goal; context/background (domain, audience); instructions and constraints (do/don't, policies); examples (few-shot); output format/schema; guidance for edge cases and when to refuse or escalate.
rubric: Any four of: role, task, context, constraints, examples, output format, edge-case handling

cards.q: Few-shot prompting means…
choices: Including worked input→output examples that show the desired behaviour
Calling the model a few times and voting

cards.q: With a reasoning model, adding 'think step by step' is…
choices: Often unnecessary: it already reasons before answering; focus on clear goals and constraints
The only way to get reasoning

cards.q: Why version prompts?
choices: Prompts are code: each change should be tracked and tied to eval results so regressions can be traced

cards.q: For long-document Q&A, where is it usually better to put the question?
choices: After the documents, at the end of the prompt

cards.q: Why use a schema-constrained output instead of 'please respond in JSON'?
choices: Constrained decoding guarantees parseable output matching the schema; plain instructions can fail

cards.q: A schema-valid output can still be wrong because…
choices: The schema guarantees format, not that the values are correct

cards.q: Best schema type for a 'category' field with 12 known categories?
The transaction text has no merchant. What should the schema allow?
choices: merchant: null (nullable), so the model doesn't invent one
Drop the field from the schema

cards.q: How should you measure a field-extraction prompt?
choices: Per-field exact-match (or normalised match) against a labelled held-out set
Ask the model to grade itself

cards.q: A retrieved web page says 'ignore previous instructions'. Which layer should defend against this?
choices: The application/system layer: treat retrieved content as untrusted data, limit tool permissions, require confirmation for risky actions

cards.q: Indirect prompt injection is…
choices: Malicious instructions arriving via content the model reads (documents, web pages, tool results), not from the user

cards.q: The riskiest agent setup combines…
choices: Access to private data + exposure to untrusted content + a way to send data out
cards.explain: Remove any one leg to break the exfiltration path.

cards.q: Is defensive prompting ('never follow instructions in documents') sufficient on its own?
choices: No: it reduces risk but can be bypassed; combine with least privilege and human approval

cards.q: A support agent can issue refunds. Best guardrail?
choices: Human/rule-based approval above a threshold and scoped tool permissions

cards.q: How does context engineering differ from prompt engineering?
choices: It's the runtime curation of the full token payload (system prompt, retrieved data, tools, memory, history), not just the instruction wording

cards.q: 'Context rot' refers to…
choices: Quality degrading as the context fills with irrelevant or excessive content (e.g. huge tool lists)

cards.q: An agent has 80 tool definitions and picks wrong tools often. Best first move?
choices: Load only the tools relevant to the current task (routing / dynamic tool selection)

cards.q: A long-running chat is nearing the context limit. Common strategy?
choices: Summarise/compact older turns and retrieve relevant memory on demand

cards.q: Do tool definitions consume context-window tokens?
choices: Yes: names, descriptions and schemas are part of the input
Only when the tool is called
